one_liner: C++ symbolic algebra core (expand, diff, series, subs, lambdify) that runs SymPy-style workloads 10x to 1000x faster than pure-Python SymPy.
what_it_does: SymEngine is a standalone C++ library for symbolic manipulation: expression trees of reference-counted Basic nodes with canonical Add/Mul/Pow, expansion, differentiation, series, substitution, matrices, polynomials, number theory and numeric evaluation (double, MPFR, MPC). It is a separate API, not a drop-in for SymPy: you use it from C++, through the C wrapper (cwrapper.h), or through symengine.py, SymEngine.jl, Ruby and Haskell wrappers, and convert to and from SymPy objects when you need SymPy's wider feature set (simplify, solvers, integration).
how_it_is_fast: Expressions are compiled C++ objects with intrusive, non-atomic reference counting (its own RCP in Release mode instead of Teuchos::RCP), hashed canonical Add/Mul stored as coefficient dictionaries, and exact coefficients on GMP, FLINT or Boost.Multiprecision integers, so construction and canonicalisation cost what SymPy pays in Python object overhead and its cache. Hot kernels are specialised: polynomial expansion over coefficient maps (the canonical expand((x+y+z+w)^n) benchmark), series over univariate polynomial types, numeric evaluation by a C++ visitor, and lambdify through LambdaRealDoubleVisitor (a tree interpreter with optional CSE) or an LLVM JIT visitor when built WITH_LLVM.
when_to_use: Python or Julia code where SymPy's expand, diff, subs or series dominates run time on expressions of hundreds to thousands of terms (the SciML run shows about 1000x on diff of a 1326-term expansion and 226x on expand((x+y+z+w)^32)).
Generating many derivatives or Jacobians for code generation (mechanics, chemical kinetics, optimal control) where symbolic construction cost matters more than simplification power.
Embedding a symbolic engine in a C or C++ application through a small MIT-licensed library with a stable C API.
Fast numeric callbacks from symbolic expressions via the lambda visitors, where SymPy's numpy lambdify call was about 12x slower per call (CSE case) on the page.
when_not_to_use: You need SymPy's breadth: simplify, solve, integrate, assumptions on expressions (issue #2047 is open) or pretty printing variants; SymEngine covers a subset and you round-trip to SymPy for the rest.

Pure-Julia pipelines on Symbolics.jl: SymbolicUtils.jl beat SymEngine on the same page for sparse-rule substitution (0.000593 s vs 0.00110 s), variable search (0.00049 s vs 0.00103 s) and compiled calls (3.13e-7 s vs 6.93e-7 s with CSE; 2.56e-6 s vs 1.07e-5 s without), partly because SymEngine is reached through ccall wrappers.
Multithreaded use of a default build: WITH_SYMENGINE_THREAD_SAFE defaults to off (on only with BUILD_FOR_DISTRIBUTION or OpenMP), so reference counts are not atomic.

Untrusted or exotic inputs where a crash is unacceptable: Release mode uses manual reference counting and raw pointers and the README says a bug can segfault; past issues include parser crashes on invalid strings (#2002) and a sparse-matrix crash (#1694).

integration.form: static lib by default (BUILD_SHARED_LIBS OFF), shared lib optional; Python, Julia, Ruby and Haskell wrappers in separate repos
integration.dependencies: GMP by default (INTEGER_CLASS gmp; or gmpxx, flint, piranha, or boostmp to drop GMP); optional MPFR, MPC, FLINT, ARB, LLVM, GMP-ECM, primesieve, TCMalloc, OpenMP; vendored cereal and Teuchos
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (target_compile_features cxx_std_11), C++17 when built with LLVM 16+; CMake 3.18+
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS and Windows (conda-forge and Conan packages, MinGW and MSVC builds); open issue #1975 reports test_fields failing on Apple M2
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe by default; build with WITH_SYMENGINE_THREAD_SAFE=yes (atomic reference counts; forced on with OpenMP), which the README recommends for distribution packages but turns off in its 'optimized build' recipe
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: symengine.py mirrors a SymPy-like API subset and converts to and from SymPy objects, and SymPy's USE_SYMENGINE=1 backend switch (sympy/core/backend.py) is used only by sympy.liealgebras in SymPy 1.14; everything else needs code changes

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the largest ratio: the eval_double row (SymEngine 0.0117 s vs SymPy 31.06 s, about 2660x) times the page's Python evaluator, which walks the tree with sympy.postorder_traversal, a recursive 'yield from' generator whose cost grows with nodes times depth. Rerun here with SymPy 1.14.0 on an Intel Xeon at 2.1 GHz, the 10000-deep expression (80,002 nodes) took 39.6 s, of which 38.1 s was the traversal alone (0.28, 1.23 and 5.33 s at depths 1000, 2000 and 4000: quadratic), while the same per-node SymPy calls driven by an explicit stack, as the page's own Julia evaluator does, took 0.184 s with the identical value 9.856474171370099. Against a linear traversal SymEngine's lead is roughly 12x to 16x (derived; cross-machine estimate), not 2660x.

The random-expression substitution builds SymPy's tree with evaluate=False constructors, so SymPy's subs re-canonicalises every rebuilt node inside the timed region. Rerun here, the tree reproduced the page's 8498 nodes; subs took 1.55 s (dense) and 0.61 s (sparse) on it versus 1.03 s and 0.46 s on a tree built with evaluating constructors (8703 nodes), so that choice inflates SymPy by about 1.3x to 1.5x on top of the unequal tree sizes (3271 SymEngine nodes) already noted.

The measured libsymengine is the prebuilt SymEngine_jll 0.12.0 with WITH_SYMENGINE_THREAD_SAFE=yes and no TCMalloc or LLVM, three releases behind 0.15.0; the README's optimized recipe (-march=native -O3, TCMalloc, thread safety off) should be faster, so SymEngine's numbers are not its best case.
The README warns that benchmark timings depend on the order benchmarks run in one executable because of malloc behaviour, and recommends TCMalloc when benchmarking.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The siblings in this category (FLINT, mp++, GMP alternatives such as Malachite or dashu) speed up numeric big-integer and polynomial arithmetic; pick SymEngine when the workload is symbolic expression manipulation (expand, diff, subs, series, codegen) and you want those exact coefficients handled for you, optionally on top of FLINT via INTEGER_CLASS=flint.
verified_claims_summary: SciMLBenchmarks (SymEngineComparison, AMD EPYC 7502, Julia 1.13.0, SymEngine.jl 0.13.2 over prebuilt libsymengine 0.12.0, SymPy unpinned via CondaPkg) measured SymEngine faster than SymPy on all ten summary workloads, from about 11x (variable search on dissimilar expressions) to about 1000x (diff of a 1326-term expansion) and 2000x (dense-rule substitution on unequal trees); the 2660x eval_double ratio is mostly SymPy's quadratic recursive-generator traversal in the page's own evaluator. SymbolicUtils.jl beat SymEngine on four rows.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-04; latest release v0.15.0), MIT-licensed with BSD-3 vendored code and packaged on conda-forge and Conan, so easy to adopt; build it with thread safety on if you share expressions across threads.
sources_read: https://pypi.org/project/sympy/ (sympy 1.14.0 wheel installed in a scratch directory to rerun the eval_double and substitution workloads, and to read sympy/core/backend.py)
